query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the powder bed during additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce thermal gradients, thereby minimizing compositional segregation, residual stress buildup, and defect formation while improving overall mechanical integrity relative to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high‐entropy alloy powder feedstock prepared for additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled preheating step for the powder bed (or build platform) during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: Processing via a typical laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) system at a preheat temperature optimized (e.g., on the order of several hundred °C, subject to further calibration to avoid undesirable phase transitions) and under standard atmospheric or inert atmosphere conditions; measurements performed in as-built state and after standard post-processing heat treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during solidification promote a more homogeneous microstructure with less compositional segregation and lower concentrations of microcracks or void defects.
generation.mechanism: Preheating decreases the differential cooling rates and thus thermal contraction mismatches. This slows down the rate of phase separation, reduces residual stresses generated by rapid cooling, and minimizes the conditions that foster defect nucleation during layer-wise deposition, which in turn improves the mechanical integrity of the final component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, samples processed with a powder-bed preheating step are expected to exhibit lower residual stresses, finer and more uniform microstructural features (reduced segregation), and fewer internal defects, leading to enhanced mechanical strength and integrity.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi produced via conventional bulk fabrication or standard additive manufacturing without preheating.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within additive manufacturing processes where thermal control is critical, and for compositions similar to AlCrFeNiSi processed under comparable atmospheres and laser processing conditions. It may not apply if preheat temperatures induce unexpected phase transformations or if the alloy system is altered significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature and its precise impact on each competing mechanism (segregation vs. residual stresses vs. defect formation) remain to be fully quantified; the magnitude of improvements in mechanical properties is directionally expected but not precisely predictable without experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using an identical LPBF system: one set with the implemented powder bed preheating and one set without (the control). Ensure that all other processing parameters remain constant. Post-fabrication, subject both sets to identical heat treatment procedures if applicable.
measurements: Residual stress measurements via X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction.
Microstructural analysis (via scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to assess chemical homogeneity and defect density.
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and hardness tests) to evaluate mechanical integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in residual stresses, compositional segregation, and defect densities—and if mechanical integrity (e.g., yield strength, ductility) does not improve relative to controls—the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
